newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.N. arms inspector arrives in Baghdad.
newsitem.headline: U.N. arms inspector arrives in Baghdad.

text.p: A senior United Nations weapons inspector arrived in Baghdad on Friday to discuss with Iraqi authorities the monitoring of weapons of mass destruction in line with 1991 Gulf War ceasefire terms.

Deputy chairman of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of scraping Iraq's prohibited weapons Charles Duelfer confirmed that Iraq last week obstructed efforts to study parts of Scud missiles.
Rolf Ekeus, chairman of UNSCOM, was quoted on Friday as saying the previously unannounced incident occured on November 15 and led to friction between the two sides.

"(Deputy Prime Minister) Tareq Aziz blocked our team as they were trying to transport the missile parts to our centre in Baghdad after digging them out of the ground," Ekeus told the United Arab Emirates English-language daily The Gulf Today.
"Iraq has denied the commission the removal of engines of these missiles that is a direct contradiction of (Security Council) resolution 687," Duelfer said.
But he said he would not discuss the missile issue because the "Iraqi side made it clear that it wished to discuss that between deputy prime minister (Aziz) and ambassador Ekeus".
"My visit...has to do with the monitoring system," Duelfer told reporters on his arrival to Rasheed hotel in the centre of the Iraqi capital.
Ekeus said he had written a letter to Aziz, saying that Iraq violated resolution 687 which calls on it to yield possession on any mass destruction weapons for removal.
Duelfer said Ekeus would visit Baghdad in early December.
Duelfer will have talks with the head of the Military Industrialisation Commission Dhaif Abdul-Majeed and other officials.
Iraq has given the U.N. a list of hundreds of missiles, launch vehicles and other weapons it said it had destroyed and buried in July 1991, few months after the end of the war over Kuwait.
Terms of the ceasefire ban Iraq from having missiles with a range greater than 150 km (94 miles) and the means to produce them.
"There was a period in 1991 when Iraq conducted a unilateral destruction...We sought to verify the number and types of missiles in fact included in the (Iraqi) declaration," Duelfer said.
Ekeus has said Iraq was still concealing as many as 16 missiles.
